chapters.title: Introduction: Welcome to the Strategy Room
chapters.summary:
Every year executives enter the strategy room armed with spreadsheets and leave with plans destined to miss their hockey-stick promises. The introduction frames the problem: strategy fails less from lack of analytics than from social dynamics - optimism, politics and the games people play to protect budgets. Drawing on McKinsey's research across thousands of companies, the authors promise two remedies: understanding the human side of strategy and using hard data on what actually drives performance.

Central to the book is the Power Curve of economic profit, which reveals brutally unequal outcomes across firms and quantifies the odds of climbing it. Strategy, they argue, should be treated as a series of bold moves with known probabilities rather than an annual planning ritual that launders wishful thinking.
chapters.takeaway: Replace annual planning theater with bold, evidence-based moves informed by real odds.

chapters.title: 1. Games in the Strategy Room—and Why People Play Them
chapters.summary:
Strategy rooms host predictable games. Business unit leaders sandbag targets to protect bonuses, anchor on last year's numbers, and negotiate budgets like arms deals. Executives confuse planning with strategy, producing documents that extrapolate current trends upward. Cognitive biases - overconfidence, loss aversion, confirmation seeking - combine with organisational politics so that plans reflect internal bargaining power rather than market realities.

The authors catalog classic manoeuvres: the sandbag, the low-ball, recycled initiatives repackaged as new, and resources spread evenly regardless of opportunity. Because everyone knows the game, cynicism replaces candour, and the result is incrementalism dressed up as ambition. Fixing strategy therefore starts with recognising that it is fundamentally a social and psychological challenge, not merely an analytical spreadsheet exercise, and redesigning the room accordingly.
chapters.takeaway: Recognise the sandbagging and politics in your strategy room before trusting its plans.

chapters.title: 2. Opening the Windows of Your Strategy Room
chapters.summary:
To see strategy objectively, open windows onto the outside world. The authors introduce the Power Curve of global economic profit: among roughly 2,400 large companies generating $1.38 trillion in total economic profit, the top decile captures about sixty-three percent, while the vast middle hovers near zero and the bottom tenth destroys value. Position on this curve determines strategic freedom: incumbents near the top enjoy momentum, while mid-curve firms must move to escape gravity.

Endowment - starting size, debt levels, past investment - shapes the odds but does not doom a company. The chapter urges leaders to benchmark themselves against this global universe rather than comfortable peer sets, converting strategy from opinion into probability. Once you know where you truly stand and what the curve demands, honest conversation about required moves becomes possible.
chapters.takeaway: Benchmark your firm against the global Power Curve to see your true strategic position.

chapters.title: 3. Hockey Stick Dreams, Hairy Back Realities
chapters.summary:
Ask any leadership team for their five-year plan and you will see a hockey stick: modest today, explosive tomorrow. Compare these projections with actual results and reality emerges as a hairy back - flat-to-volatile performance that never reaches the promised curve. Analysing hundreds of firms, McKinsey found planned profit growth systematically exceeds delivered growth by wide margins, with the gap widest for companies furthest down the curve.

Why does the delusion persist? Plans are negotiated artefacts satisfying boards and bonus schemes, not forecasts meant to come true. Optimism compounds through each planning round while nobody is accountable for the delta between slide and outcome. Breaking the pattern requires treating the hockey stick as a hypothesis to be tested against base rates and required moves, not a motivational poster.
chapters.takeaway: Test every hockey-stick plan against historical delivery rates instead of applauding optimistic curves.

chapters.title: 4. What Are the Odds?
chapters.summary:
Where a company lands is largely a matter of odds, and those odds are measurable. Endowment - starting revenue, debt, R&D spending and capital intensity relative to industry - explains much of the variance in economic-profit trajectories. But the authors' analysis shows moves matter too: firms undertaking major programmes of programmatic M&A, dynamic resource reallocation, substantial capital expenditure and productivity improvement dramatically raise their probability of ascending quintiles on the Power Curve.

A mid-tier company making one or two significant moves meaningfully improves its chances; making three or more multiplies them several-fold. This probabilistic framing liberates strategists from deterministic fatalism: endowment is destiny only if you stand still. Leaders should quantify their odds honestly, then decide deliberately whether the magnitude of moves needed is worth pursuing - or accept a humbler trajectory.
chapters.takeaway: Quantify your odds: endowment sets the baseline but bold moves change your probability of ascent.

chapters.title: 5. How to Find the Real Hockey Stick
chapters.summary:
Not all hockey sticks are lies; some strategies genuinely bend the curve. The authors offer tests separating credible plans from fantasy. Start with the outside view: what growth have similar companies in similar positions actually achieved? Check whether the plan implies winning share from competitors who are also improving, whether margins exceed anything the industry has sustained, and whether required investment fits the balance sheet.

Real hockey sticks trace to identifiable mechanisms - entering structurally growing markets, consolidating fragmented industries through repeated acquisitions, or shifting mix toward software-like economics. Each implied move must be sized, sequenced and resourced. If the projected curve exceeds what the underlying moves could plausibly deliver, the gap signals either missing moves or wishful arithmetic. Rigorous triangulation turns ambition into an executable bet with understood risks.
chapters.takeaway: Validate ambitious plans by checking implied growth against base rates and concrete resourced moves.

chapters.title: 6. The Writing Is on the Wall
chapters.summary:
Companies rarely fail from ignorance of disruption; they fail from reading the writing on the wall and doing nothing. The chapter examines how industry waves - technological, regulatory, demographic - reshape profit pools faster than incumbents respond. Kodak saw digital photography coming; newspapers watched classifieds migrate online. The pattern is rational inertia: existing customers, margins and organisation punish early movers internally even as the wave gathers force externally.

The authors urge continuous scanning of long-term trends and competitor trajectories, translating weak signals into explicit scenarios and trigger points. Crucially, responding requires asymmetric bets placed before certainty arrives, funded by reallocating from declining businesses. Boards should ask not whether trends will matter but when, and what position the company must hold if the wave breaks as expected.
chapters.takeaway: Act on structural trends early with asymmetric bets instead of waiting for certainty.

chapters.title: 7. Making the Right (Big) Moves
chapters.summary:
Analysis of thousands of companies identifies five categories of moves that reliably lift firms up the Power Curve: programmatic M&A executed as serial, capability-building deals; dynamic resource reallocation shifting capital toward promising businesses annually; substantial capital expenditure matched with capital-efficiency gains; productivity improvement exceeding industry pace; and genuine differentiation in pricing, innovation or business model. Magnitude matters as much as category - reallocating a token few percent barely registers.

Companies making one or two big moves materially improve their odds; three or more raise the likelihood of reaching the top quintile severalfold. The chapter profiles firms that combined moves into coherent strategies sustained over years. The message is uncomfortable for consensus cultures: meaningful ascension demands concentrated, courageous commitments rather than many small, safe initiatives scattered across the portfolio.
chapters.takeaway: Make three or more big concentrated moves across M&A, reallocation, capex, productivity and differentiation.

chapters.title: 8. Eight Shifts to Unlock Strategy
chapters.summary:
The closing chapter prescribes eight shifts to unlock strategy. Move from annual planning events to strategy as an ongoing journey; from straight-line extrapolation to scenario-based lateral thinking; from a narrow industry sandbox to a wide-angle view of ecosystems, technology and global competitors; from recycled playbooks to deliberately sourced fresh perspectives; from bias-laden debate to structured de-biasing tools; from painting by numbers to boundary-breaking ambition; from siloed functional plans to integrated full-potential views of each business; and from fear-driven conformity to cultures where dissent and candour are rewarded.

None requires genius - they require redesigned routines, different questions and leaders willing to hear uncomfortable answers. Practised together, the shifts turn the strategy room from theatre into a decision factory that consistently generates and executes the big moves the Power Curve demands.
chapters.takeaway: Redesign strategy routines around journeys, scenarios, wide lenses and candour to enable big moves.
